text: I spent years building the perfect poker face, and I was wrong about it.
Not about what it is, about what it does to the people around you,
because a neutral face doesn't look neutral to everyone else.
It looks sad, angry, bored, sometimes even arrogant.
Today we're skipping the basics everyone already knows.
No, stay calm and breathe.
We're covering what happens in real life when your face stays blank,
and how to fix it without faking a single emotion.
If you already know what a poker face is, skip ahead 20 seconds.
Everyone else, here's the short version.
A poker face is a steady expression that gives nothing away.
poker players use it so opponents can't read their hand.
In daily life it means your face looks the same,
whether the news is good or bad, not blank, steady.
Sounds like pure advantage, right?
Nobody can read you, nobody can use your emotions against you.
That's exactly what I believed, until a simple question kept showing up.
Picture this, you're in a meeting, you're relaxed, maybe even enjoying it.
Afterwards, someone walks over an arsex.
Hey, are you okay? Did I do something?
You did nothing, you felt nothing, but they saw something.
And this is the part most people miss.
When a face gives no information, people don't leave the gap empty.
They fill it, attentive people especially.
They notice your face doesn't match the moment,
and their brain writes a story to explain it.
Research on neutral faces suggests they're often read as carrying a motion,
and it's usually a negative one.
So a calm face becomes, he's upset, or she's judging me, or he doesn't like me.
So the poker face that was supposed to give you control, quietly handed the narrative to everyone else.
You wanted to be unreadable, what you became is easy to miss read,
which raises the real question. If hiding everything backfires is the answer to show everything.
No, that's the opposite mistake, and it has its own cost. The answer is much smaller than that.
Neutral and unreadable are two different things. You don't need to add a motion.
You need to add signals.
Start with your baseline. Most people who look angry while feeling calm are holding tension
without knowing it, jaw-clenched, forehead tight, eyes locked,
relax the jaw, unclenched the forehead, let the corners of your mouth rest very slightly up.
It should feel like doing nothing, but it reads as calm instead of cold.
Then give one small signal in every interaction. A nod, a brief eyebrow lift when someone speaks.
A quick, got it. It's tiny, but it tells the other person you're engaged, and that alone removes most of the guessing.
Then use your voice. When your face stays still, tone does the work. A slightly slower
warmer voice fixes more misreads than any facial trick.
And there's one more fix that takes two seconds, but most people are too proud to use it.
We'll get to it in a moment, because first you need to know how to keep all of this stable.
Steady doesn't mean rigid. Rigid is what people read as cold, so check your tension points regularly.
Jaw, forehead, eyes. A locked face looks like anger even when you feel nothing.
The best way to test this is to record yourself on a voice or video call. Then watch it back
with the sound off. Write down what a stranger would guess you're feeling. It's uncomfortable,
but it's the fastest way to see the gap between how you feel and how you look.
Now here's something that should take pressure off. Research on the illusion of transparency,
suggests we overestimate how visible our emotions are to others, which means you probably need
less control than you think. Most people aren't studying your face. The ones who are,
are the ones who ask the questions. And they will ask. So let's fix that.
The rule is one calm sentence, no defensiveness, no long explanation. Over-explaining
looks like guilt, and it makes the other person more suspicious, not less. If someone asks,
are you sad? Say, no, I'm good. My face just goes flat when I'm thinking.
If they ask, are you angry or irritated? Say, not at all. This is just my default face.
If I'm annoyed, you'll know. If it, do you not like me? Say, it's not that.
I'm just not very expressive. Honestly, I'm enjoying this.
If someone calls you cold or a narcissist, say, reserved, not cold, I take time to open up.
Then, back it up with one warm action, like asking them a real question about themselves.
Actions beat explanations every time. That's the two second fix I mentioned. Say what your face
isn't saying. I'm just thinking, or I'm focused, not annoyed. It prevents the wrong story before
it starts. Now the last question. The one people ask when they can't read you at all.
Are you kind or evil? And it's fair, because of face, can't answer that. Neither can
sense it. So you say, watch what I do, not how I look. Then you make sure your actions match.
Which brings us back to the title. What I got wrong was thinking a poker face means showing nothing.
It doesn't. The real skill is showing exactly what you choose to show.
Keep the poker face for high stakes moments like conflict, negotiation and provocation.
Drop it everywhere else. Try one thing this week, record one conversation, watch it silently,
and write down what a stranger would guess. That single note will teach you more than any technique
I gave you today.
